text:
Sean Gallagher: Kicking off “hot-route capacity protection” workstream. This is the thing we’ve been circling since the Dec + early Jan overloads. Goal: a small number of routes/tenants can’t take down the fleet. We need tier-aware admission control + clear 429 semantics + routing lanes.

Sean Gallagher: Context (recent pain):
- Dec 18: retry storm from 1 enterprise client on `chat.completions` -> regional queue depth spiked, p99 blew out, spillover 5xx on unrelated traffic
- Jan 08: kernel regression reduced effective tok/s; we kept accepting traffic until routers fell over
- Jan 12: bursty embed route + delayed metering -> quota enforcement inconsistent, support got hammered w/ “why am I getting random 429s”

Rafael Mendes: +1. And the Jan 08 event had the worst property: “everything is slow everywhere” even though the demand was concentrated in 2 top routes.

Aisha Bello: For dashboards: we currently only have global throttles + a couple per-model graphs. Need per-route/per-tier throttled_count and saturation signals if we want to page sanely.

Talia Benson: Thanks Sean. I’m program-leading this (per Priya). I’ll keep this thread for kickoff notes + owners + initial SLO targets. We’ll convert into a Linear umbrella after we align.

Priya Natarajan: Exec sponsor here. Please bias toward something shippable in phases. We can’t block the product roadmap for a perfect scheduler, but we *can* stop one route from cascading.

Sean Gallagher: Proposed high-level plan (very rough):
1) Gateway: per-tenant+route+region rate limits + standardized 429 payloads
2) Router: priority lane for enterprise (bounded fairness so self-serve isn’t fully starved)
3) Backpressure: ingest runtime signals (queue depth/prefill saturation) -> shed traffic earlier
4) SLOs + alerts tied to enterprise hot routes

Mina Haddad: On routing side: we can do separate queues by lane. The open question is strict priority vs weighted fair queue. Strict priority is simplest but we need a starvation bound or we’ll never drain self-serve during incidents.

Amara Diallo: Gateway can do per-route keys. Need to agree on what “route” means (path vs path+model?) and what we expose in headers. Also: do we want rate limit limits to be “requests/sec” or “tokens/sec”? tokens/sec at gateway is hard.

Cole Summers: Quota enforcement: metering is delayed by design (few mins). If we hard fail on quota during metering lag, we’ll false-throttle. If we fail open, we risk overages during incidents. We need explicit policy: fail-open but cap bursts? (or conservative local counters).

Sofia Ivanova: Runtime side: GPU util alone is noisy. Queue depth + prefill saturation are the most reliable “we’re in trouble” signals. We can sample every ~2s without much overhead. Decode saturation per-model is harder.

Vikram Singh: Data plane integration: router can consume a “saturation score” and adjust admission. But please keep label cardinality under control if you’re emitting per-route metrics from the data plane.

Allison Grant: 👋 observability standards note: per-route *can* be OK if route set is bounded + we don’t include tenant_id as a label. For tier, keep it to a small enum (enterprise/self_serve/internal).

Sergio Costa: +1. If you put tenant_id in Prom labels I will personally revert the PR :)

Sean Gallagher: lol noted.

Sean Gallagher: Let’s define “hot routes” as a small explicit allowlist (maybe 10-20) that gets special handling + dashboards + SLOs. Everything else uses global defaults.

Talia Benson: Ownership (initial):
- SRE overall / SLOs / rollout: Rafael + Sean
- Gateway rate limits + 429 standardization: Amara
- Smart routing / priority lanes: Mina
- Quota semantics / billing hooks: Cole
- Backpressure signals / runtime inputs: Sofia + Vikram
- Observability standards + dashboards: Allison + Sergio + Aisha
- Feature flags / staged rollout: Benji

Benji Okafor: Feature flag side: we can gate by region + by “route group” (hot routes first). Need a config schema to avoid hand-editing YAML in prod.

Aisha Bello: Proposed SLO targets for “enterprise hot routes” (starting point, please throw rocks):
- Availability: 99.9% monthly (exclude explicit 429 OverCapacity?)
- Latency: p95 <= 1.5s (prefill+first token), p99 <= 3.0s for chat; embeddings p95 <= 500ms
- Throttling: during incidents, we’d rather return 429 quickly than slow 200s

Rafael Mendes: Important: we need to define whether 429 counts against availability SLO for enterprise. For self-serve it’s fine; for enterprise we may have contractual expectations.

Priya Natarajan: For enterprise: a 429 is still “we didn’t serve the request.” If we’re using 429 as a protection mechanism, we need to be explicit in contracts + docs. But I agree fast 429 is better than timeouts.

Mina Haddad: Maybe treat 429 OverCapacity as a separate budgeted category. Like: primary availability SLO counts 5xx/timeouts; secondary “capacity SLO” measures 429 rate and has its own thresholds.

Sean Gallagher: That’s aligned with how we’ve done “graceful degradation” elsewhere. Also helps avoid gaming: “we’re up because we 429’d everything.”

Amara Diallo: On semantics: can we standardize on:
- HTTP 429
- `Retry-After: <seconds>`
- JSON body with `code`, `message`, `policy`, `request_id`
- And maybe a header like `x-redwood-throttle-reason`

Cole Summers: Please add a reason code that distinguishes “rate_limit” vs “quota” vs “over_capacity” vs “config_error”. Support needs this.

Aisha Bello: +1. Also for dashboards: reason_code breakdown is super useful.

Sofia Ivanova: Runtime can provide “over_capacity” reason if admission is based on saturation. But quota/rate-limit is gateway-level.

Vikram Singh: Router can attach reason if it sheds due to backpressure. But we should avoid leaking internal details (like queue depth values) in customer-visible bodies.

Allison Grant: Re: labels: reason_code can be a label if we keep the set bounded and stable. Don’t put raw policy strings in labels.

Incident Bot: (FYI) Incident retrospective snippet from #incidents Jan 08 linked: “Capacity dip + uncontrolled retries caused p99 > 20s. Routers accepted traffic until thread pools exhausted.”

Rafael Mendes: Action items I’m hearing:
1) Define initial hot-route list (top enterprise endpoints) + tier definitions
2) Agree SLO shape (availability vs capacity SLO) + paging signals
3) Draft ADR for routing model (strict priority + bounded fairness vs W-FQ)
4) Draft ADR for quota/rate limit semantics + fail-open/closed policy

Talia Benson: Yep. I’ll schedule a 45m this week with Mina/Amara/Cole/Sofia + SRE to settle: tier enum, hot-route list, and SLO definitions. I’ll post notes back here.

Sean Gallagher: One more thing: we need explicit rollback/kill switch requirements. When this misbehaves, oncall needs a single flag to disable lane enforcement without redeploy.

Benji Okafor: Will include “kill switch” in flag design. Also: config validation + safe defaults. If config fetch fails, I strongly prefer fail-open for enterprise lane and fail-closed for self-serve? (open to debate)

Rafael Mendes: Careful: fail-open globally can melt the fleet. Maybe: fail-open for *existing* limits (use cached config) and fail-closed only for new/unknown routes.

Amara Diallo: Gateway can cache last-known-good config and enforce it for N minutes. If cache is empty, default to conservative global limits.

Priya Natarajan: This is the right direction. Keep it explainable. If we’re throttling, customers should see consistent behavior and clear Retry-After guidance.

Aisha Bello: I’ll start a draft dashboard spec: throttled_count by route group + lane utilization + queue depth + p95/p99 by tier. Will share early so we can sanity check cardinality.

Sean Gallagher: Great. Please keep updates in this thread until we have the Linear umbrella + Confluence page. :thumbsup:
